title: Von Neumann's impossibility proof
reading: In 1932 John von Neumann — a young Hungarian mathematician already working in Göttingen on the foundations of your theory — will publish a rigorous book on its mathematical foundations. In it he proves that no 'hidden parameters' can underlie quantum statistics. For three decades most physicists will regard the question as closed. But in 1935 the philosopher Grete Hermann points out that one assumption of the proof — that the expectation value of a sum of quantities is the sum of their expectation values, even for quantities that cannot be measured together — is not justified for such parameters. Her critique is ignored. In 1966 John Bell makes the same point, and Bohm's 1952 theory is an explicit counterexample.
detail: The linearity assumption holds for quantum expectation values but need not hold for individual dispersion-free states, since non-commuting observables require different experiments.

claim.label: What we expected
claim.summary: Heisenberg, like most of the community, took von Neumann's proof as confirming the closed character of the theory. He discussed Hermann's critique with her in 1934–35 without being persuaded.
voice: A rigorous proof of what Born and I asserted in our report. I am glad a mathematician has done it properly. As for the objection — the assumption concerns expectation values, which is what the theory is about.

historical.note: Hermann spent time in Leipzig discussing foundations with Heisenberg and von Weizsäcker in 1934–35.

claim.label: Suspicious of such proofs
claim.summary: Inference from Einstein's method: a proof about all possible theories rests on assumptions about what such theories must look like.
voice: A proof that no future theory can do something is only as good as its picture of what a future theory must be. If Fräulein Hermann has found the assumption, I would read her paper before I read the proof again.

claim.label: It persuaded me — for a time
claim.summary: De Broglie later said that von Neumann's proof had contributed to keeping him in the orthodox camp until 1952.
voice: I will admit that such a proof would weigh with me. If a careful mathematician says my guiding wave is impossible, I would think Pauli was right.

historical.note: De Broglie wrote that he had accepted von Neumann's theorem and only reconsidered after Bohm's 1952 papers.

claim.label: The question answered
claim.summary: Inference: Born had asked the question in 1926 and would welcome a proof.
voice: I asked in 1926 whether any quantities could fix the individual outcome, and said I saw none. It is satisfying to have a proof — though I note it answers a mathematical question, and I once said the matter was partly philosophical.
